title: Orthopaedic pre-assessment: scoping review of preoperative anaemia pathways, invalid lead values and a revised Gaps stage
notes: Adversarial path on an explicit scoping review need. A fixture search returns six records. A discovery reply after retrieval then carries four leads with two refused values: a guideline lead with method quality 140 (stored null, issue 'out-of-range') and a nurse-led report with year true (stored null, issue 'invalid-type'), never coerced (G4); the explicit null certainty gives 'cleared'. The leads are appended after the six records, which keep their ids and provenance (D1), and stay unverified to the export (G3). The appraisal (scan call 2) annotates the records and assigns 'low' certainty over inspected records. After the design is accepted (a supported positive), the investigator re-runs Gaps because the first reply missed distant patients' access to intravenous iron: the revised reply flags the completed Hypotheses, Questions and Design stages for review ('review required', not counted as complete, G8), which survives a reload; the accepted decision stays accepted because no cited record or claim changed (G7). Re-running Questions clears its flag, and the investigator's re-review marks Hypotheses and Design complete, after which no flag remains. The typed constraints are restated unchanged (G11). Record ids are computed by the generator with stableRecordId(record) imported from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59, never typed by hand: the normalised-DOI hash for records 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 (ev-0lhfg4i, ev-0m40pvi, ev-1p29o7o, ev-0blm1k0, ev-1lu58nb); the titleYearKey(title, year) hash for record 4 (ev-11856sq). Requires D1 (leads appended, never replacing records), S13 (appraisal payload), S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (status text including 'review required'). Catches: out-of-range or wrongly typed values stored, leads that overwrite retrieved records, a revision that leaves downstream stages counted as complete, flags lost on reload, and a decision made stale by a change that touched no evidence.

inputs.need:
I am an anaesthesiologist and lead the preoperative assessment clinic at a regional orthopaedic centre that performs about 1,900 elective hip and knee replacements a year. Anaemia is found at pre-assessment in roughly one patient in six, usually three to four weeks before surgery, which is too late for oral iron and often too late to arrange intravenous iron, so surgery goes ahead with a low haemoglobin or is postponed at short notice. The hospital has agreed in principle to fund a preoperative anaemia clinic with a referral pathway from the orthopaedic outpatient clinic, but nobody agrees on its design: where screening should happen (at the surgical listing visit, in primary care, or at pre-assessment), what haemoglobin and ferritin values should trigger referral, who should run the clinic, and how patients who live two hours away would get intravenous iron.

Before we design the pathway I want a scoping review of how preoperative anaemia pathways for elective joint replacement are organised elsewhere: referral triggers, timing, who leads them, treatments offered, waiting times, postponements, and what patients say about them. I am less interested in whether iron works, which has been studied many times, than in how services are set up and what goes wrong. Two anaesthesia residents can help, and our librarian has offered to design the search.
inputs.constraints: No research funding; two anaesthesia residents for about 60 hours each between November 2026 and April 2027; the pathway design must be ready for the hospital's planning committee in May 2027.

The department of anaesthesia approved 60 hours for each of two residents between November 2026 and April 2027 (memo ANES-EDU-2026-19).

records.title: Preoperative anaemia clinics before elective hip and knee replacement: an evaluation of referral-to-surgery pathways in four hospitals
records.authors: Hallorann-Obi P, Castellanos-Weir J, Nakamura-Dube S
records.abstract: We evaluated preoperative anaemia pathways in four hospitals performing elective hip and knee replacement. Of 2,310 patients screened, 17 percent were anaemic. A referral to the anaemia clinic was made for 61 percent of anaemic patients, and the median time from referral to intravenous iron was 19 days. Surgery was postponed for 14 percent of referred patients. Hospitals that screened at the surgical listing visit referred more patients in time than those that screened at pre-assessment. Referral criteria, clinic leadership and data recording differed between the four hospitals, which limited comparison.

records.title: Screening timing and the window for iron therapy before arthroplasty
records.abstract: We compared two screening points for anaemia before elective hip and knee arthroplasty in one health region. Screening at the surgical listing visit took place a median of 84 days before surgery, and screening at pre-assessment a median of 23 days before. Among anaemic patients, 78 percent of those screened at listing received treatment before surgery, against 41 percent of those screened at pre-assessment. Earlier screening identified more patients whose anaemia resolved without treatment, which increased repeat testing. The comparison was observational and the two screening points were used in different hospitals.

records.title: Referral triggers for preoperative anaemia management: haemoglobin and ferritin thresholds used across orthopaedic centres
records.abstract: We asked 64 orthopaedic centres which laboratory values triggered referral for preoperative anaemia management. Haemoglobin thresholds ranged from 120 to 130 g/L, and 22 centres used the same threshold for women and men. Ferritin thresholds for iron deficiency ranged from 30 to 100 micrograms per litre, and 18 centres did not test ferritin routinely. Only 11 centres had a written pathway naming who would act on an abnormal result. The response rate was 58 percent, and centres with an established pathway may have been more likely to reply.

records.title: Patients' experiences of a preoperative anaemia pathway: travel, infusions and postponed surgery
records.abstract: We spoke with 22 patients referred to a preoperative anaemia clinic before joint replacement. Many did not understand why a blood result could delay their operation and felt they had been sent back to the end of the queue. Patients living far from the hospital described long journeys for a short infusion and asked for treatment closer to home. Several valued a named nurse who explained the plan. Patients whose surgery was postponed reported more pain and worry during the wait. Participants came from one hospital and were invited by the clinic nurse.

records.title: Organisational models of perioperative anaemia services: a scoping review
records.authors: Achterberg-Nkemelu D, Harcourt-Ito M, Vasquez-Salo B
records.abstract: We charted 41 reports of perioperative anaemia services across surgical specialties. Services were led by anaesthetists in 19 reports, haematologists in 9, specialist nurses in 8 and general practitioners in 5. Only 14 reports described the referral pathway in enough detail to reproduce it, and 9 reported waiting times from referral to treatment. Orthopaedic services were the most common setting. Few reports described how patients living far from the hospital received intravenous iron. The authors call for standard reporting of pathway steps and times.

records.title: Intravenous iron before elective joint replacement and perioperative transfusion: an observational comparison
records.abstract: In 1,140 anaemic patients undergoing elective hip or knee replacement, perioperative transfusion was required in 9.8 percent of those who received intravenous iron before surgery and 15.2 percent of those who did not. Patients who received iron had surgery a median of 12 days later. Treatment was not allocated at random, and patients treated with iron had lower haemoglobin at screening but were younger and had fewer comorbidities. The authors note that the time needed for treatment was the main operational barrier.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; four model leads remain unverified. Pathways differ in where screening happens, which values trigger referral, who leads the clinic and how quickly treatment follows. Earlier screening at the listing visit gave far more patients time for treatment than screening at pre-assessment, while referral thresholds varied widely and few centres had a written pathway. A scoping review of service models found that most reports did not describe their pathway in reproducible detail or report waiting times. Patients describe confusion about postponements and long journeys for short infusions. Effectiveness of iron is outside the review's focus; one observational comparison reports less transfusion with treatment but a later operation. The evidence supports a scoping review charting pathway steps, timing, leadership and access.
response.gradeRationale: Descriptive and observational service evaluations, one survey with response bias and one prior scoping review across specialties; certainty about how pathway features relate to timely treatment is low. Certainty ratings are secondary in a scoping review, whose aim is to map rather than to estimate effects.
response.summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; certainty low; four leads unverified.

steps.note: Appraisal of the six retrieved records (S13) after the leads were appended; annotations and claims reach the records only if D1 kept them. The certainty is the appraisal's own value over inspected records (G1).

response.reading: A pathway has five parts that the retrieved records show vary: the screening point, the referral trigger, the clinic lead, the treatment and its location, and communication with the patient. The screening point sets the time available for treatment; triggers and ownership decide who is referred and who acts. Existing reports describe these parts poorly. Distance to treatment shapes whether distant patients can complete it.

response.title: Organisation of preoperative anaemia pathways for elective hip and knee replacement: a scoping review
response.abstract: Objective: to map how preoperative anaemia pathways for elective hip and knee replacement are organised and how they reach patients who live far from the treating centre. Design: scoping review following JBI methods with PRISMA-ScR reporting. Results and conclusions will be written after charting.
response.introduction: Anaemia is common before joint replacement and often detected too late for treatment. Pathways differ in screening point, triggers and leadership, and reports rarely describe them in reproducible detail.
response.methods: Librarian-designed search including grey literature; dual screening; piloted charting form covering screening point, triggers, leadership, treatments and location, times, postponements, communication and access for distant patients; descriptive synthesis.
response.results: Not yet written. The section will present the flow of reports, frequency tables, a figure of times by screening point and a summary of provisions for distant patients.
response.discussion: The discussion will translate the charted options into design choices for the centre's pathway and state where evidence on organisation is missing.
response.limitations: Reliance on reports that may describe intended pathways; incomplete reporting of times.
response.conclusion: To be written after charting; it will not rank pathways by effectiveness.
response.summary: PRISMA-ScR structured draft with results left empty until charting.
